clue.text: Hardy's man was not the same

definitions.meaning: Thomas Hardy's story collection is titled A — Man and Other Tales

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a Hardy character was never the same again.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's title figure is an altered man, and to have altered is to have become different from before.

clue.text: Royal barge used in romance?

parts.note: the royal court is the monarch's household
a barge is a kind of vessel

explanation.surface: A royal barge serves as the setting for a love affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used in' is a link; the question mark flags that a royal barge is literally a court vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooing someone with a view to marriage is a romance, a love affair in progress.

clue.text: One of Tolstoy's rank, say, in narrative

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is to be spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: Leo Tolstoy was a Russian count, so one of his rank is a count, a nobleman

explanation.surface: A Tolstoy-like nobleman features in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks a homophone: 'a count' spoken sounds like the word for a narrative; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrative is a report or story of events, as in an eyewitness's version of what happened.

clue.text: Tomasi's patriot takes the biscuit

definitions.meaning: the Italian unification hero whose campaign is the backdrop to Tomasi di Lampedusa's The Leopard
a British biscuit with a layer of squashed currants, named after that same hero

explanation.surface: A patriot from an Italian novel wins the prize for audacity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes the biscuit' is a British idiom meaning surpasses everything; here it is a link plus the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Risorgimento general appears in The Leopard, and a British currant biscuit bears his name.

clue.text: It accompanied me in Ustinov work

definitions.text: It accompanied me in Ustinov work

parts.words: It accompanied me in Ustinov work
parts.note: Peter Ustinov's autobiography has a two-word title whose second word is me; the clue asks for the word paired with it

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what went alongside 'me' in a book by Peter Ustinov.
explanation.definitionFit: Ustinov's memoir is titled with an affectionate exclamation followed by the word me.

clue.text: Sir Osbert recorded one in Egypt

definitions.text: Sir Osbert recorded one in Egypt

parts.words: Sir Osbert recorded one in Egypt
parts.note: Sir Osbert Sitwell wrote a novel about a supernatural wonder on the Sinai peninsula, in Egypt

explanation.surface: Osbert Sitwell wrote down an extraordinary event that happened in Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitwell's novel concerns a wonder on Sinai, a supernatural event beyond natural explanation.

clue.text: His works are little read, and rarely scanned

definitions.text: His works are little read, and rarely scanned

parts.words: His works are little read, and rarely scanned
parts.note: describes the Scottish versifier famed as the worst poet in English, whose lines seldom scan metrically

explanation.surface: An obscure writer is neither widely read nor closely examined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scanned' looks like 'studied closely' but means 'had regular metre'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian Dundee rhymester is notorious for doggerel whose metre limps.

clue.text: Lawrence disguise I recognized in The Eternal City

parts.note: T. E. Lawrence enlisted in the RAF under the assumed name Ross

explanation.surface: Lawrence of Arabia, in disguise, is spotted in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: The Eternal City looks like Rome, but here it is Hall Caine's novel of that name, whose hero is David Rossi.
explanation.definitionFit: David Rossi is the central character of Hall Caine's novel The Eternal City.

clue.text: I am in church period, looking for The Beast

indicators.note: the shortened form of I am sits inside the other letters

parts.note: an era is a period of history
contracted to I'm

explanation.surface: Someone in church searches through an era for the Beast of Revelation.
explanation.definitionFit: The fire-breathing monster of Greek myth, part lion, part goat, part serpent, is a fabulous beast.

clue.text: "I am the — you killed, my friend" (Wilfred Owen)

definitions.text: "I am the — you killed, my friend" (Wilfred Owen)

parts.words: "I am the — you killed, my friend" (Wilfred Owen)
parts.note: the missing word from a line in Wilfred Owen's poem Strange Meeting, spoken by a dead German soldier

explanation.surface: A line from a First World War poem with one word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Strange Meeting the dead speaker is the foe, the opposing soldier, whom the poet killed.

clue.text: "An eight-man on a four-job, and all four-s — working" (Harry Truman)

definitions.text: "An eight-man on a four-job, and all four-s — working" (Harry Truman)

parts.words: "An eight-man on a four-job, and all four-s — working" (Harry Truman)
parts.note: Truman's quip about stress names a stomach sore throughout; the blanks all take that one word

explanation.surface: Harry Truman joking about a stressed official with too much worry.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR has dropped the blanks before 'man' and 'job': the quotation is an eight-[blank] man on a four-[blank] job.
explanation.definitionFit: A stomach sore is the classic stress ailment, so Truman counted a worrier's burden in them.

clue.text: In Britain he reportedly represented the Roman, see?

definitions.text: In Britain he reportedly represented the Roman, see?

parts.words: In Britain he reportedly represented the Roman, see?
parts.note: the monk Pope Gregory sent to convert the English in 597, who became the first archbishop of Canterbury, a see of Rome

explanation.surface: A question about who stood for Rome in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see' looks like 'understand?' but is a bishop's diocese: he represented the Roman see, the papacy.
explanation.definitionFit: The saint sent from Rome founded the see of Canterbury and was the Pope's envoy to Britain.

clue.text: The witch's pricked

parts.note: in Macbeth a witch says 'By the pricking of my' digits, 'something wicked this way comes'

explanation.surface: A witch's something was pricked.
explanation.definitionFit: The second witch in Macbeth senses evil by a prickling in her short thick digits.

clue.text: How beautiful was Auden's living creature?

definitions.text: How beautiful was Auden's living creature?

parts.words: How beautiful was Auden's living creature?
parts.note: in Auden's Lullaby the sleeping lover is a living creature who is to the poet wholly beautiful

explanation.surface: A question about the beauty of a creature in an Auden poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Auden's line calls the beloved the wholly beautiful, so the word means completely.

clue.text: Poet encouraged to go on the wagon

definitions.meaning: John ..., the English Georgian poet and playwright

definitions.text: encouraged to go on the wagon
definitions.meaning: being told to give up alcohol, i.e. advised to stick to soft beverages

explanation.surface: A poet is urged to stop drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go on the wagon' is an idiom for giving up alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: John Drinkwater was a Georgian poet; a teetotal adviser would tell you to take only tap liquid.

clue.text: Elizabeth Bowen's was fully booked before Arthur Haley's

definitions.text: Elizabeth Bowen's was fully booked before Arthur Haley's

parts.words: Elizabeth Bowen's was fully booked before Arthur Haley's
parts.note: Bowen's first novel (1927) and Arthur Hailey's bestseller (1965) share this one-word title

explanation.surface: Bowen's establishment was full before Hailey's ever opened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fully booked' sounds like a full house of guests, but means made into a book: Bowen's novel came first.
explanation.definitionFit: Both novels are named for an inn, a place where guests pay for lodging.

clue.text: Household name, Herries perhaps?

parts.note: Geoffrey Household's thriller title; Hugh Walpole's Rogue Herries would be an example of such a man

explanation.surface: A question about whether Herries is a well-known name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Household name' looks like a celebrity but is a title by the novelist Geoffrey Household; Walpole's Rogue Herries is a male rogue.
explanation.definitionFit: Household's novel is named for a dangerous loner, like a solitary elephant, and Herries is a scoundrel man.

clue.text: Fringe benefit for Irish novelist

parts.note: a fringe is an edge or border
worth is value or benefit

explanation.surface: An Irish writer enjoys a perk on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fringe benefit' reads as a job perk; split, it gives the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Edgeworth wrote Castle Rackrent and is a major Anglo-Irish novelist.

clue.text: Modern composer in topless boot

indicators.note: the first letter of the boot's name is removed

parts.note: a wellington is a rubber boot, commonly called a welly in Britain

explanation.surface: A contemporary composer stands in a boot with its top cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: Duke Ellington was a twentieth-century jazz composer and bandleader.

clue.text: Strange Pisa salon revealing sufferings of the saints

indicators.note: the strange arrangement of the letters of Pisa salon signals that they are mixed up

explanation.surface: An odd salon in Pisa shows pictures of martyred saints.
explanation.definitionFit: A book recounting the martyrdoms and torments of saints, read on their feast days.

clue.text: Crime writer hidden in some inn

indicators.note: the letters of some inn are disguised, rearranged to conceal the writer

explanation.surface: A crime novelist is lying low in an inn somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hidden' here signals a rearrangement, not letters in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Georges Simenon, Belgian creator of Inspector Maigret, wrote detective novels.

clue.text: Agate protagonist from Swanage, Melbourne, or London

indicators.note: the letters come out of the run of words Swanage, Melbourne

explanation.surface: A character in a novel by James Agate hails from one of several towns.
explanation.walkthrough: James Agate's 1928 novel is titled Gemel in London, so 'or London' points at the title.
explanation.definitionFit: James Agate, the drama critic, wrote a novel whose central figure is named in its title.

clue.text: Provenance of Clarence's last drink

parts.note: the Duke of Clarence was drowned in a butt of malmsey, a sweet wine from an Atlantic island

explanation.surface: Where the Duke of Clarence's final drink came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Malmsey is a sweet fortified wine from that Portuguese Atlantic island.

clue.text: A bully of his acquaintance was skilfully reconstructed after rugby (3, )

definitions.text: A bully of his acquaintance was skilfully reconstructed after rugby

parts.words: A bully of his acquaintance was skilfully reconstructed after rugby
parts.note: the schoolboy hero of Thomas Hughes's Rugby School novel knew the bully Flashman, later revived in George MacDonald Fraser's novels

explanation.surface: A bully someone knew was rebuilt after a rugby match.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby is the school, not the game; Flashman, the bully, was skilfully reconstructed in Fraser's Flashman novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Hughes's schoolboy hero at Rugby is tormented by Flashman, whom Fraser later made his own hero.

clue.text: Most of prose stylist is unexpressed ()

indicators.note: all but the last couple of letters of the historian's name are kept

parts.note: Tacitus, the Roman historian famous for his terse prose

explanation.surface: Most of a writer's prose remains unspoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Something understood without being stated is implied, never voiced.

clue.text: The Hebrew Dante appears in eerie Titian work

indicators.note: the name shows up inside the words eerie Titian

explanation.surface: Dante in a Hebrew guise turns up in a spooky Titian painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' is a link; Moses Rieti, a 15th-century Italian Jewish poet, was called the Hebrew Dante.
explanation.definitionFit: Moses Rieti wrote a Hebrew poem modelled on the Divine Comedy, earning the nickname.

clue.text: Davis Cup team made philosophical by the presence of Borg

definitions.text: Davis Cup team made philosophical by the presence of Borg

parts.words: Davis Cup team made philosophical by the presence of Borg
parts.note: Bjorn Borg's national tennis side; add his surname and you get the mystic philosopher Emanuel ...

explanation.surface: A tennis nation's team becomes reflective with Bjorn Borg in its ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: Borg was the Scandinavian tennis star; adding BORG to the country gives Swedenborg, the philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Borg played Davis Cup for his Scandinavian homeland, and that land plus his name is a philosopher.

clue.text: Image said to be not working

indicators.note: the word for not working is spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: idle means not working

explanation.surface: A picture is reported to be broken.
explanation.definitionFit: A graven figure worshipped as a god is an image.

clue.text: "If you are foolish enough to be —, don't show it …" (Jerome K. Jerome)

definitions.text: "If you are foolish enough to be —, don't show it …" (Jerome K. Jerome)

parts.words: "If you are foolish enough to be —, don't show it …" (Jerome K. Jerome)
parts.note: Jerome's advice continues 'but grumble with the rest'; the missing word is happy with one's lot

explanation.surface: A Jerome K. Jerome line advising against showing satisfaction.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome's ironic advice is to hide being satisfied and grumble like everyone else.

clue.text: A revel of Ralph? ()

parts.note: Ralph ... Doister, the early English comedy, has a hero whose name is built on an old verb meaning to carouse

explanation.surface: A question about Ralph's carousing.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic verb to riot or carouse underlies Ralph Roister Doister's swaggering name.

clue.text: Possibly get Rain in African port

indicators.note: possibly signals that get Rain may be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: There may be rain in an African harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moroccan city on the Strait of Gibraltar is a major North African seaport.

clue.text: Song heard introducing German novelist is in fact a British one

indicators.note: a word for a song is spoken, giving a sound spelt differently

parts.note: a lay is a song or ballad
Thomas Mann, author of The Magic Mountain

explanation.surface: A song introduces a German novelist who turns out to be British.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a British one' means a British novelist: Rosamond Lehmann, author of Dusty Answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosamond Lehmann was an English novelist, author of Dusty Answer and The Weather in the Streets.
